- **D)** AWS Glue

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

Amazon Quick Sight (formerly Amazon QuickSight, now part of Amazon Quick) is a serverless, machine learning-powered business intelligence (BI) service that lets you create interactive dashboards and visualizations. It connects to multiple data sources including S3, Redshift, RDS, Athena, and more. Athena runs SQL queries on S3 data but does not provide visualization dashboards. ### Question 239 (`CLF-U1663`) [point:compute_ec2_spot_interruptible]

A startup expects unpredictable traffic spikes for a new mobile app. The company does not want to commit to a long-term contract. Which EC2 pricing model is MOST appropriate?

On-Demand Instances let you pay by the second (or hour) with no upfront commitment or long-term contract. This is ideal for unpredictable workloads. Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment. Spot Instances can be interrupted with short notice, making them risky for user-facing apps. Dedicated Hosts are for compliance-driven workloads and are the most expensive option.

### Question 240 (`CLF-U1664`) [point:compute_ec2_spot_interruptible]

A company has a stable, predictable database workload that will run continuously for the next three years. Which pricing option will provide the GREATEST cost savings?

- **A)** On-Demand Instances
- **B)** Spot Instances
- **C)** Reserved Instances with All Upfront payment for 3 years
- **D)** Reserved Instances with No Upfront payment for 1 year

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

Reserved Instances with a 3-year term and All Upfront payment offer the highest discount (up to 72% off On-Demand). The longer the commitment and the more you pay upfront, the greater the discount. 1-year No Upfront still saves money but less than 3-year All Upfront. Spot Instances are interruptible, so they are unsuitable for a database. On-Demand is the most expensive option for sustained workloads.

### Question 241 (`CLF-U1665`) [point:compute_ec2_spot_interruptible]

A data analytics team needs to run a large batch processing job that can tolerate interruptions. Which EC2 pricing model offers the DEEPEST discount?

- **A)** On-Demand Instances
- **B)** Savings Plans
- **C)** Spot Instances
- **D)** Reserved Instances

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount compared to On-Demand pricing, making them the cheapest option. However, AWS can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when it needs the capacity back. This makes them ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch processing, data analysis, and CI/CD pipelines. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances offer up to 72% savings but require commitments.

*Sources: OpenExamPrep_Questions*

</details>

### Question 264 (`CLF-U1893`) [point:compute_ec2_spot_interruptible]

A company runs an uninterruptible Amazon EC2 workload on AWS 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. <details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

#### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Options A and B: ✅ Why they are CORRECT:** **Standard Reserved Instances** provide the highest discount rate (up to 72%) when instance family, OS, and region remain unchanged for the duration. Combining Standard RIs with an **All Upfront** payment option delivers the maximum possible cost savings over 12 months. - **Option C: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Spot Instances can be interrupted at any time, making them unacceptable for an uninterruptible 24/7 mission-critical workload. - **Option D: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Convertible Reserved Instances offer flexibility to change instance families during the term, but provide lower discounts than Standard RIs when instance configurations are fixed. - **Option E: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Compute Savings Plans offer broad cross-service flexibility (EC2, Fargate, Lambda), but lower discounts than instance-locked Standard RIs paying all upfront. ---

### Question 265 (`CLF-U1895`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

According to the AWS shared responsibility model, who is responsible for the virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities in which AWS services operate? #### Options - **A.** It is the sole responsibility of AWS. **[CORRECT]** - **B.** The customer's AWS Support plan tier determines who manages the configuration. - **C.** It is the sole responsibility of the customer. - **D.** It is a shared responsibility between AWS and the customer.


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

#### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A: ✅ Why it is CORRECT:** Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, AWS is responsible for "Security OF the Cloud". This includes the physical facilities, hardware, network infrastructure, host hypervisors, and virtualization layer across all regions and data centers. - **Option B: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Support tiers provide varying levels of technical guidance and response times, but do not alter the fundamental boundaries of the Shared Responsibility Model. - **Option C & D: ❌ Why they are INCORRECT:** Customers have zero physical or hypervisor access in the cloud; physical security and virtualization are exclusively handled by AWS. ---

*Sources: FreeCram_Questions*

</details>

### Question 266 (`CLF-U1901`) [point:compute_elastic_beanstalk_paas]

<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

The developer simply uploads application code, and Elastic Beanstalk automatically provisions EC2 instances, load balancers, auto-scaling groups, and database bindings. - **Option A: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Amazon EC2 is an Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) offering requiring manual provisioning and configuration of operating systems, security groups, web servers, and runtime stacks. - **Option C: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS CodeBuild compiles source code, runs automated unit tests, and produces deployable artifacts, but it does not deploy or maintain application hosting environments. - **Option D: ❌ Why it is INCORRECT:** Amazon Personalize is a managed machine learning service for real-time recommendation engines, unrelated to general web application deployment. ---

### Question 293 (`CLF-U2206`) [point:srm_aws_hardware_facility]

**Topic:** `Cloud computing benefits` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Multiple` **Question ID:** `cdb9a99b-f7a3-4481-b032-2536bebf1a87` > **Scenario *(Select TWO)*:** > Which are common benefits of cloud computing? (Select TWO.) #### Options - **A.** Rapid global deployment **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Reduced need to manage physical infrastructure **[CORRECT]** - **C.** Guaranteed zero downtime - **D.** Elimination of all security responsibilities - **E.** Unlimited free capacity


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** Two fundamental benefits of cloud computing are deploying globally in minutes and shifting the burden of managing physical infrastructure to the cloud provider. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Rapid global deployment allows organizations to deploy applications in multiple AWS Regions around the world with just a few clicks or API calls. - **Option B:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Reduced need to manage physical infrastructure eliminates the heavy lifting of racking, stacking, powering, and cooling physical hardware in data centers. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Guaranteed zero downtime is impossible in any IT environment; AWS provides high availability architectures but never guarantees 100% zero downtime. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, customers remain responsible for security 'in' the cloud (data, IAM, guest OS, network configurations). - **Option E:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Cloud capacity is vast and elastic, but it is not completely unlimited nor is it free; usage incurs metered costs. --- <a id="q-9"></a>

### Question 294 (`CLF-U2207`) [point:srm_customer_os_patching_ec2]

**Topic:** `AWS shared responsibility model` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `11435e9b-8626-4f3e-9b61-edcd0c178d65` > **Scenario:** > Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is generally the customer's responsibility for an Amazon EC2 instance? #### Options - **A.** Patching the guest operating system **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Replacing failed physical disks - **C.** Securing AWS data centers - **D.** Maintaining the hypervisor


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** In Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) like Amazon EC2, customers are responsible for managing the guest operating system, including security updates and patches. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Patching and updating the guest operating system (Linux or Windows) on Amazon EC2 instances is strictly the customer's responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Replacing failed physical storage drives and hardware components is AWS's responsibility as part of security 'of' the cloud. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Securing physical data centers, facilities, perimeters, and environmental controls is entirely managed by AWS. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Maintaining and patching the virtualization hypervisor layer (such as AWS Nitro) is the responsibility of AWS. --- <a id="q-10"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

### Question 295 (`CLF-U2208`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

**Topic:** `AWS shared responsibility model` | **Difficulty:** `Easy` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `bbff97a4-1a33-48c7-9f8b-1bfb60b72978` > **Scenario:** > Which security task remains the customer's responsibility when using Amazon S3? #### Options - **A.** Configuring bucket policies **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Maintaining S3 storage hardware - **C.** Patching the S3 service - **D.** Guarding AWS facilities

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

### Question 297 (`CLF-U2210`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

**Topic:** `AWS shared responsibility model` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Multiple` **Question ID:** `965fb1b5-f0ce-491b-8514-7167cbbb1ec2` > **Scenario *(Select TWO)*:** > Which responsibilities remain with the customer in AWS? (Select TWO.) #### Options - **A.** Managing IAM permissions **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Classifying and protecting application data **[CORRECT]** - **C.** Securing AWS data center buildings - **D.** Replacing failed AWS networking hardware - **E.** Maintaining the AWS hypervisor

### Question 298 (`CLF-U2215`) [point:compute_ec2_spot_interruptible]

**Topic:** `Amazon EC2` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `dbae6b2c-3a46-4fae-a716-2d5422779137` > **Scenario:** > A workload requires a predictable amount of compute capacity continuously for three years. Which EC2 purchasing option can provide a discount in exchange for a commitment? #### Options - **A.** Reserved Instances **[CORRECT]** - **B.** On-Demand Instances - **C.** Spot Instances - **D.** Dedicated Hosts without a commitment

> **Summary:** Reserved Instances (RIs) and Compute Savings Plans provide significant discounts (up to 72%) in exchange for a committed steady-state usage term of 1 or 3 years. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Reserved Instances provide substantial cost savings for predictable, steady-state workloads running continuously over a 1-year or 3-year commitment period. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** On-Demand Instances provide maximum flexibility with no commitment, but carry the highest hourly cost for steady, continuous workloads. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a 2-minute warning and are unsuitable for continuous, interruption-sensitive production applications. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Dedicated Hosts without commitments incur high hourly rates and are primarily intended for dedicated hardware licensing requirements, not standard cost reduction. --- <a id="q-18"></a>

### Question 299 (`CLF-U2219`) [point:compute_ec2_dedicated_compliance]

**Topic:** `AWS Lambda` | **Difficulty:** `Easy` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `91f9cb17-b3e8-43e3-9a79-949320ce3dfb` > **Scenario:** > A developer needs to run short-lived code whenever a new object is uploaded to an S3 bucket. Which service is best suited? #### Options - **A.** AWS Lambda **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Amazon EC2 Dedicated Host - **C.** Amazon RDS - **D.** AWS Direct Connect


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events (such as S3 object creation) and automatically manages the underlying compute resources. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** AWS Lambda allows developers to run short-lived, event-driven functions automatically triggered by S3 `s3:ObjectCreated:*` events without managing servers. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** EC2 Dedicated Hosts require managing physical servers and maintaining continuous operating costs, which is unsuitable for event-driven short-lived code. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service, not a serverless compute execution environment. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS Direct Connect establishes dedicated private network connections between on-premises data centers and AWS, not code execution. --- <a id="q-22"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

### Question 300 (`CLF-U2222`) [point:comp_cloudtrail_api_governance]

**Topic:** `AWS Lambda` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Multiple` **Question ID:** `54121e98-afa8-4841-bb64-d62c3dd42d7f` > **Scenario *(Select TWO)*:** > Which are characteristics of AWS Lambda? (Select TWO.) #### Options - **A.** AWS manages the underlying servers. **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Functions can be invoked by events or direct API calls. **[CORRECT]** - **C.** Customers must choose and patch an operating system. - **D.** Functions run indefinitely without execution limits. - **E.** Every function requires a permanently running EC2 instance.


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** AWS Lambda is a fully managed serverless compute service where AWS handles server infrastructure and functions are triggered by events or direct API calls. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** AWS manages all underlying infrastructure, server provisioning, operating system maintenance, capacity scaling, and high availability. - **Option B:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Lambda functions can be triggered automatically by events from over 200 AWS services (e.g., S3, DynamoDB, SQS) or invoked directly via API Gateway and SDK calls. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Customers do not manage, select, or patch the underlying operating system in AWS Lambda; it is managed entirely by AWS. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Lambda functions have a hard maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes (900 seconds) and cannot run indefinitely. - **Option E:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Lambda is serverless and executes in temporary, managed micro-containers; it does not require running permanent EC2 instances. --- <a id="q-25"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

### Question 301 (`CLF-U2239`) [point:compute_elb_traffic_distribution]

**Topic:** `Elastic Load Balancing` | **Difficulty:** `Easy` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `6a23f106-3fc9-4519-996f-3d50de6ac608` > **Scenario:** > A web application runs on multiple EC2 instances and needs automatic distribution of incoming HTTP traffic. Which service should be used? #### Options - **A.** Application Load Balancer **[CORRECT]** - **B.** NAT gateway - **C.** AWS Transit Gateway - **D.** Amazon EBS


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and routes traffic based on URL paths, host headers, and HTTP request attributes across EC2 targets. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Application Load Balancer operates at the application layer (Layer 7) and provides advanced content-based routing (e.g., path/host routing) for HTTP and HTTPS workloads. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** A NAT gateway translates private IPv4 addresses to a public address for outbound internet egress, not load balancing. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS Transit Gateway acts as a central cloud router connecting hundreds of VPCs and on-premises networks, not an HTTP application load balancer. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Amazon EBS is a persistent block storage service, not a network traffic distribution service. --- <a id="q-42"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

---

### Question 302 (`CLF-U2240`) [point:compute_elb_traffic_distribution]

**Topic:** `Elastic Load Balancing` | **Difficulty:** `Hard` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `e29a2a3d-f66a-44a3-8b6d-4c7e6ff31c0a` > **Scenario:** > A company needs to distribute TCP traffic to a fleet of servers while preserving very high throughput and low latency. Which load balancer is most appropriate? #### Options - **A.** Network Load Balancer **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Application Load Balancer - **C.** Gateway Load Balancer only for HTTP routing - **D.** CloudFront origin access control


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 (Transport layer) and is capable of handling millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency while preserving client IP addresses. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS) and provides ultra-low latency, handling volatile traffic patterns and massive throughput. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and inspects application-layer HTTP protocols, which incurs slightly higher latency than Layer 4 NLB. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Gateway Load Balancers deploy and scale third-party virtual network appliances (like firewalls and IDS/IPS), not standard TCP application server fleets. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** CloudFront origin access control (OAC) secures access between CloudFront distributions and S3 origins, not TCP server load balancing. --- <a id="q-43"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

### Question 303 (`CLF-U2242`) [point:compute_elb_traffic_distribution]

**Topic:** `Elastic Load Balancing` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Multiple` **Question ID:** `15f846ff-3c95-494c-a8c3-3b5b8c3231c7` > **Scenario *(Select TWO)*:** > Which statements about Elastic Load Balancing are correct? (Select TWO.) #### Options - **A.** It can distribute traffic across multiple Availability Zones. **[CORRECT]** - **B.** It can integrate with Auto Scaling groups. **[CORRECT]** - **C.** It replaces all application authentication controls. - **D.** It provides persistent block storage to targets. - **E.** It automatically makes every backend application stateless.


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

> **Summary:** Elastic Load Balancing distributes incoming application traffic across targets in multiple Availability Zones and integrates seamlessly with EC2 Auto Scaling. #### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** ELB can balance incoming application traffic across targets deployed in multiple Availability Zones, enhancing fault tolerance and resiliency. - **Option B:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** ELB automatically registers and deregisters instances managed by EC2 Auto Scaling groups as the fleet expands or contracts based on demand. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** ELB does not replace application authentication or authorization controls; application logic or IAM/Cognito is still required. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** ELB is a network routing and balancing service; it does not provide persistent storage to compute targets. - **Option E:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** ELB does not alter backend application state; developers must architect applications to be stateless or use external session stores. --- <a id="q-45"></a>

*Sources: SecByte_Questions*

</details>

**Topic:** `AWS pricing models` | **Difficulty:** `Medium` | **Type:** `Single` **Question ID:** `bc03cc78-43ae-40d4-bd99-262a52f6bd77` > **Scenario:** > Which pricing model is most appropriate for a fault-tolerant workload that can be interrupted and restarted? #### Options - **A.** Spot pricing **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Dedicated Host pricing only - **C.** On-Demand pricing with no interruptions allowed - **D.** Data transfer pricing

### Question 305 (`CLF-U2279`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

**Classification:** `Domain 2: Security and Compliance` | `Subdomain 2.1: Understand the AWS shared responsibility model.` **Origin:** *Live Quiz Engine (ID: 80433)* > **Scenario:** > Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for the physical security of the data centers hosting AWS services? #### Options - **A.** AWS is responsible for physical security, including controlling access to the data center facilities and hardware. **[CORRECT]** - **B.** The customer is responsible for physical security, since AWS only manages the software layer of its services. - **C.** The customer's compliance team audits and enforces physical access controls inside AWS data center buildings. - **D.** AWS delegates physical facility security to the customer through a shared responsibility matrix agreement.

<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

#### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Physical facility security, including controlling who can access data center buildings and hardware, is part of security of the cloud and is entirely AWS's responsibility. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS manages hardware and physical infrastructure, not just software; customers never take on physical data center security under this model. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Customers do not have physical access to AWS data centers and cannot audit or enforce access controls inside AWS facilities. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** There is no mechanism by which AWS hands physical facility security to a customer; this responsibility remains with AWS across all services. ---

### Question 306 (`CLF-U2281`) [point:srm_customer_os_patching_ec2]

**Classification:** `Domain 2: Security and Compliance` | `Subdomain 2.1: Understand the AWS shared responsibility model.` **Origin:** *Live Quiz Engine (ID: 80440)* > **Scenario:** > An attacker exploits an unpatched vulnerability in the guest operating system of a customer's EC2 instance. Under the shared responsibility model, whose gap in duties allowed this exposure? #### Options - **A.** The customer's gap, since guest operating system patching for EC2 instances is a customer responsibility. **[CORRECT]** - **B.** AWS's gap, since AWS is responsible for patching every guest operating system running on EC2 instances. - **C.** AWS Inspector's gap, since it is responsible for automatically patching vulnerable guest operating systems. - **D.** AWS Shield's gap, since it is responsible for blocking exploitation attempts against unpatched guest systems.


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

#### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Because EC2 leaves guest operating system patching with the customer, an unpatched vulnerability at that layer reflects a gap in the customer's own security-in-the-cloud duties. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS does not patch guest operating systems on EC2 instances, so this exposure cannot be attributed to an AWS patching failure. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and reports findings, but it does not apply patches itself, so it cannot be responsible for the unpatched state. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** AWS Shield mitigates distributed denial-of-service attacks; it plays no role in patching or protecting against guest operating system vulnerabilities. ---

*Sources: CertSafari_Questions*

</details>

### Question 307 (`CLF-U2310`) [point:compute_lambda_serverless_execution]

**Classification:** `Domain 3: Cloud Technology and Services` | `Subdomain 3.4: Identify AWS database services.` **Origin:** *Live Quiz Engine (ID: 80658)* > **Scenario:** > A small engineering team runs a PostgreSQL database on a self-managed EC2 instance and spends significant time each month applying OS patches, testing minor version upgrades, and configuring backup scripts. They want to keep the same PostgreSQL engine but remove this operational burden. What should they do? #### Options - **A.** Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, which handles patching, upgrades, and automated backups **[CORRECT]** - **B.** Move the EC2 instance to a larger instance type so the existing patch and backup scripts run faster - **C.** Replace the relational schema with Amazon DynamoDB tables and rewrite the application queries entirely - **D.** Keep the EC2-hosted database and schedule an AWS Lambda function that applies patches automatically each week


<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

#### Comprehensive Verification & Explanations - **Option A:** ✅ **Why it is CORRECT:** Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL is a fully managed relational database service, so AWS handles operating system patching, engine version upgrades, and automated backup scheduling on behalf of the customer. - **Option B:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Resizing the EC2 instance only changes compute and memory capacity; the team would still own every patching, upgrade, and backup task on the instance. - **Option C:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** Switching to DynamoDB changes the data model to NoSQL and would require rewriting the application logic, which is a far bigger change than the team needs just to remove patching overhead. - **Option D:** ❌ **Why it is INCORRECT:** A custom Lambda-based patch scheduler still requires the team to build, test, and maintain the automation themselves, so the operational burden of a self-managed database remains. ---

*Sources: CertSafari_Questions*

</details>

### Question 340 (`ACTUAL-393-Q025`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which activity can companies complete by using AWS Organizations?

- **A)** Troubleshoot the performance of applications.
- **B)** Manage service control policies (SCPs).
- **C)** Migrate applications to microservices.
- **D)** Monitor the performance of applications.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: )</b></summary>

Managing service control policies (SCPs) is an activity that companies can complete by
using AWS Organizations. AWS Organizations is a service that enables the user to
consolidate multiple AWS accounts into an organization that can be managed as a single
unit. AWS Organizations allows the user to create groups of accounts and apply policies to
them, such as service control policies (SCPs) that specify the services and actions that
users and roles can access in the accounts. AWS Organizations also enables the user to
use consolidated billing, which combines the usage and charges from all the accounts in
the organization into a single bill3.

*Sources: Consensus_Aligned, Amazon_CLF_C02_Nov2026_Recall_393Q*

</details>

### Question 346 (`ACTUAL-393-Q075`) [point:iam_identity_center_sso]

AWS IAM Access Analyzer can identify and report unused access granted to IAM users
and roles. When an unused-access analyzer is created, it reviews access activity and
generates findings for conditions such as unused roles, unused IAM user access keys,

investigations, but it does not by itself produce the specialized unused-access findings
described in the question. IAM Identity Center centrally manages workforce access to
multiple AWS accounts and applications but is not the analysis service for identifying
unused IAM permissions. AWS Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks across
categories such as cost, performance, resilience, security, and servic

*Sources: Consensus_Aligned, Amazon_CLF_C02_Nov2026_Recall_393Q*

### Question 347 (`ACTUAL-393-Q100`) [point:iam_role_temporary_credentials]

A company has teams that have different job roles and responsibilities. The company's
employees often change teams. The company needs to manage permissions for the
employees so that the permissions are appropriate for the job responsibilities.
Which IAM resource should the company use to meet this requirement with the LEAST
operational overhead?

- **A)** IAM user groups
- **B)** IAM roles
- **C)** IAM instance profiles
- **D)** IAM policies for individual users

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: )</b></summary>

IAM roles are a way of granting temporary permissions to entities that need to access
AWS resources, such as users, applications, or services. IAM roles allow customers to
assign permissions to entities without having to create or manage IAM users or credentials
for them. IAM roles can be assumed by different entities depending on the trust policy
attached to the role. For example, IAM roles can be assumed by IAM users in the same or
different AWS accounts, AWS services such as EC2 or Lambda, or external identities such
as federated users or web identities. IAM roles can also be switched by IAM users to
temporarily change their permissions. IAM roles are recommended for managing
permissions for employees who often change teams, because they allow customers to
define permissions based on job roles and responsibilities, and easily assign or revoke
them as needed. IAM roles also reduce the operational overhead of creating, updating, or
deleting IAM users or credentials for e

*Sources: Consensus_Aligned, Amazon_CLF_C02_Nov2026_Recall_393Q*

### Question 348 (`ACTUAL-393-Q107`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

Which task requires the use of AWS account root user credentials?

- **A)** The deletion of IAM users
- **B)** The change to a different AWS Support plan
- **C)** The creation of an organization in AWS Organizations
- **D)** The deletion of Amazon EC2 instances

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: )</b></summary>

The creation of an organization in AWS Organizations requires the use of AWS account
root user credentials. The AWS account root user is the email address that was used to
create the AWS account. The root user has complete access to all AWS services and
resources in the account, and can perform sensitive tasks such as changing the account
settings, closing the account, or creating an organization. The root user credentials should
be used sparingly and securely, and only for tasks that cannot be performed by IAM users
or roles4

*Sources: Consensus_Aligned, Amazon_CLF_C02_Nov2026_Recall_393Q*

</details>

### Question 350 (`ACTUAL-393-Q155`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

Which of the following actions are controlled with AWS Identity and Access Management

access to AWS services and resources securely. You can use IAM to perform the following
actions:
Control access to AWS service APIs and to other specific resources: You can create
users, groups, roles, and policies that define who can access which AWS resources and
how. You can also use IAM to grant temporary access to users or applications that need to
perform certain tasks on your behalf3 Protect the AWS environment using multi-factor
authentication (MFA): You can enable MFA for your IAM users and root user to add an
extra layer of security to your AWS account. MFA requires users to provide a unique
authentication code from an approved device or SMS text message, in addition to their
user name and password, when they sign in to AWS4

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: )</b></summary>

Server-side encryption is an encryption option that Amazon S3 provides to encrypt data at
rest in Amazon S3. With server-side encryption, Amazon S3 encrypts an object before
saving it to disk in its data centers and decrypts it when you download the objects. You
have three server-side encryption options to choose from: SSE-S3, SSE-C, and SSE-KMS.

own encryption keys. SSE-KMS uses keys that are managed by AWS Key Management

### Question 369 (`CLF-U0017`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

Which of the following must an IAM user provide to interact with AWS services using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)?

- **A)** Access keys.
- **B)** Secret token.
- **C)** UserID.
- **D)** User name and password.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A)</b></summary>

**Correct answer: Access keys**

To interact with AWS services using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), an IAM user must configure the AWS CLI with their access key ID and secret access key. These access keys are used to digitally sign requests to AWS, allowing the AWS services to verify the identity of the user and ensure that they have the necessary permissions to perform the requested actions. Access keys are long-term credentials for an IAM user or the AWS account root user. It is a security best practice to use IAM users instead of the root user, and to rotate access keys periodically.

**Incorrect:**

**B. User ID** - While a User ID is a unique identifier for an IAM user, it is not used for authentication with the AWS CLI. Access keys (Access Key ID and Secret Access Key) are required for authentication.

**C. User name and password** - User names and passwords are used for logging into the AWS Management Console, not for authenticating with the AWS CLI. The AWS CLI uses access keys for authentication.

**D. Secret token** - Secret tokens are used in conjunction with temporary security credentials, such as those obtained through AWS STS (Security Token Service) when assuming an IAM role. While access keys are used directly for IAM users, a secret token is used when assuming a role and is not a direct credential for an IAM user.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, ExamCert_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 370 (`CLF-U0040`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

What are the default security credentials that are required to access the AWS management console for an IAM user account?

- **A)** MFA.
- **B)** Security tokens.
- **C)** A user name and password.
- **D)** Access keys.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

**Correct answer: A user name and password**

To access the AWS Management Console using an IAM user account, you typically need a user name and password. These are the primary credentials used for authentication. When you create an IAM user, you can either generate an access key (for programmatic access via the AWS CLI, SDKs, or APIs) or enable console access, which requires setting a password. The username and password combination is the default and most common way for IAM users to log in to the AWS Management Console.

**Incorrect:**

**A. Security tokens** - Security tokens are temporary credentials used to grant limited-privilege access to AWS resources. They are often used in conjunction with IAM roles or when using multi-factor authentication (MFA), but they are not the default credentials required for logging into the AWS Management Console as an IAM user.

**B. MFA** - Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) adds an extra layer of security to your AWS account. While highly recommended, MFA is not the default credential required to access the AWS Management Console. It is an additional security measure that you can enable after you have already authenticated with your username and password.

**C. Access keys** - Access keys (access key ID and secret access key) are used for programmatic access to AWS services via the AWS CLI, SDKs, or APIs. They are not used to log in to the AWS Management Console. Access keys are used by applications or command-line tools to make requests to AWS services without requiring a user to manually enter their credentials.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, ExamCert_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 371 (`CLF-U0072`) [point:sec_macie_pii_discovery]

App development companies move their business to AWS to reduce time-to-market and improve customer satisfaction, what are the AWS automation tools that help them deploy their applications faster? (Choose TWO)

- **A)** AWS CloudFormation.
- **B)** AWS Migration Hub.
- **C)** AWS IAM.
- **D)** AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
- **E)** Amazon Macie.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A, D)</b></summary>

**Correct answer: AWS Elastic Beanstalk**

AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) that simplifies the deployment and management of web applications and services. Developers can upload their code, and Elastic Beanstalk automatically handles the infrastructure provisioning, operating system management, application deployment, and health monitoring. This allows app development companies to deploy applications faster by abstracting away the underlying infrastructure complexities.

**Correct answer: AWS CloudFormation**

AWS CloudFormation is an Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) service that allows you to define and provision AWS infrastructure as code. You create templates that describe the desired state of your AWS resources, and CloudFormation automates the creation and configuration of those resources. This enables app development companies to deploy applications faster by automating the infrastructure setup process, ensuring consistency, and reducing manual errors.

**Incorrect:**

**A. AWS IAM** - AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a service that enables you to manage access to AWS services and resources securely. While IAM is crucial for security and access control, it does not directly automate the deployment of applications. Its primary function is to define and manage user permissions and roles.

**B. Amazon Macie** - Amazon Macie is a fully managed data security and data privacy service that uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and protect sensitive data in AWS. Macie helps organizations comply with regulations and protect their data, but it does not directly contribute to the automation of application deployment.

**C. AWS Migration Hub** - AWS Migration Hub provides a central location to track the progress of application migrations to AWS. It helps you discover existing servers and applications, plan migrations, and track the status of each migration. While it aids in the overall migration process, it does not directly automate the deployment of applications once they are in AWS.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, ExamCert_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 372 (`CLF-U0113`) [point:iam_role_temporary_credentials]

A company wants to grant a new employee long-term access to manage Amazon DynamoDB databases. Which of the following is a recommended best-practice when granting these permissions?

- **A)** Create an IAM role and attach a policy with Amazon DynamoDB access permissions.
- **B)** Create an IAM role and attach a policy with Administrator access permissions.
- **C)** Create an IAM user and attach a policy with Amazon DynamoDB access permissions.
- **D)** Create an IAM user and attach a policy with Administrator access permissions.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

For a specific employee requiring long-term access, an IAM user is the appropriate identity type, and attaching a policy scoped only to Amazon DynamoDB follows the principle of least privilege by granting only the permissions needed for that role.
Creating an IAM role and attaching DynamoDB access permissions would be appropriate for applications or services that need temporary access to DynamoDB, but for a specific long-term employee, an IAM user is the correct identity type rather than a role designed for temporary credential assumption. Creating an IAM role with Administrator access permissions would grant the new employee unrestricted access to all AWS services and resources, violating the principle of least privilege and posing an unnecessary security risk. Creating an IAM user with Administrator access permissions would grant unrestricted access to all AWS services rather than scoping permissions to only Amazon DynamoDB, directly violating the principle of least privilege.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the AWS service that allows you to manage access to AWS services and resources securely. IAM enables you to create and manage AWS users and groups, and use permissions to allow and deny their access to AWS resources. A key security feature of IAM is the ability to enable MFA for users, adding an extra layer of security beyond just a username and password. **E. Amazon Connect** - Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service. It is not related to enabling or managing virtual MFA for IAM users.

### Question 374 (`CLF-U0151`) [point:sec_macie_pii_discovery]

Which of the following can help secure your sensitive data in Amazon S3? (Choose TWO)

- **A)** Delete the encryption keys once your data is encrypted.
- **B)** With AWS you do not need to worry about encryption.
- **C)** Enable S3 Encryption.
- **D)** Encrypt the data prior to uploading it.
- **E)** Delete all IAM users that have access to S3.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C, D)</b></summary>

Enabling S3 encryption through server-side encryption with S3-managed keys, KMS keys, or customer-provided keys protects object confidentiality at rest, and encrypting data before uploading it provides client-side encryption that ensures data is protected before it ever leaves the client. Both are valid approaches to securing sensitive data in Amazon S3.
Deleting encryption keys once data is encrypted would permanently prevent decryption of the stored data, making it impossible to read or use the data again; encryption keys must be retained and managed carefully to ensure continued access to encrypted data. AWS does not automatically handle all security concerns by default; customers are responsible for configuring appropriate encryption, access controls, and bucket policies to protect their data, as the shared responsibility model requires active customer participation in data security. Deleting all IAM users with access to S3 would prevent all legitimate users from accessing the data and disrupt normal operations; proper access control involves granting least privilege permissions to the appropriate users rather than eliminating all access.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 375 (`CLF-U0169`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which of the following resources can an AWS customer use to learn more about prohibited uses of the services offered by AWS?

- **A)** AWS Service Control Policies (SCPs).
- **B)** AWS Artifact.
- **C)** AWS Budgets.
- **D)** AWS Acceptable Use Policy.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: D)</b></summary>

The AWS Acceptable Use Policy outlines prohibited uses of AWS services, including activities such as sending spam, hosting illegal content, or launching attacks, and applies to all AWS customers and users.
AWS Service Control Policies are permission guardrails applied within AWS Organizations to restrict what actions accounts can perform, not a document describing prohibited uses of AWS services to external customers. AWS Artifact is a self-service portal for accessing AWS compliance reports and security documentation such as SOC reports and ISO certifications, not a resource for understanding usage restrictions. AWS Budgets is a cost management tool for setting spending thresholds and receiving alerts, unrelated to acceptable use or prohibited activities.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 376 (`CLF-U0259`) [point:general_cloud_concept]

Which of the following tasks is the responsibility of AWS?

- **A)** Encrypting client-side data.
- **B)** Configuring AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
- **C)** Securing the Amazon EC2 hypervisor.
- **D)** Setting user password policies.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

Under the shared responsibility model, AWS is responsible for securing the underlying hypervisor that runs EC2 virtual machines, as this forms part of the infrastructure layer that customers have no access to or control over.
Encrypting client-side data is the customer's responsibility, as AWS has no involvement in data that is encrypted before being sent to AWS services. Configuring IAM roles is the customer's responsibility, as customers define and manage the permissions that control what actions users and services can perform within their account. Setting user password policies is the customer's responsibility, as customers control the IAM password policies that govern how their users authenticate to the AWS Management Console.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 377 (`CLF-U0290`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which of the following AWS services provide compute resources? (Choose two.)

- **A)** AWS Lambda
- **B)** Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)
- **C)** AWS CodeDeploy
- **D)** Amazon Glacier
- **E)** AWS Organizations

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A, B)</b></summary>

AWS Lambda provides serverless compute by running code in response to events without requiring you to provision or manage servers, and Amazon ECS runs containerised applications on managed compute infrastructure. Both are purpose-built AWS compute services.
AWS CodeDeploy automates the deployment of application code to compute targets such as EC2 instances and Lambda functions, and is a deployment automation tool rather than a compute service that provides resources. Amazon S3 Glacier is an archival storage service designed for rarely accessed data with retrieval times ranging from minutes to hours, and is a storage service with no compute capability. AWS Organizations is a account management service for centrally governing and consolidating multiple AWS accounts, and has no compute capability of any kind.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>

### Question 378 (`CLF-U0317`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

The AWS Trusted Advisor checks include recommendations regarding which of the following? (Choose two.)

- **A)** Information on Amazon S3 bucket permissions
- **B)** AWS service outages
- **C)** Multi-factor authentication enabled on the AWS account root user
- **D)** Available software patches
- **E)** Number of users in the account

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A, C)</b></summary>

AWS Trusted Advisor checks S3 bucket permissions to identify those with overly permissive public access that could expose data, and verifies that MFA is enabled on the root user account, both falling under its Security checks category.
AWS service outages are tracked by the AWS Health Dashboard, which provides real-time and historical status information about AWS services across all Regions, and are not a category of checks performed by Trusted Advisor. Available software patches for EC2 instance operating systems are identified by Amazon Inspector and AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, and are not a category of recommendations provided by Trusted Advisor. The number of users in the account is visible through the IAM console and IAM credential reports, and is not a recommendation category in Trusted Advisor, which focuses on security, cost, performance, fault tolerance, and service limits.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>

### Question 379 (`CLF-U0327`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

Which service can be used to monitor and receive alerts for AWS account root user AWS Management Console sign-in events?

- **A)** Amazon CloudWatch
- **B)** AWS Config
- **C)** AWS Trusted Advisor
- **D)** AWS IAM

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A)</b></summary>

Amazon CloudWatch can monitor for root user console sign-in events through CloudTrail integration, and can be configured to send alerts via SNS when the root user logs in, enabling security teams to detect and respond to unexpected root account access.
AWS CloudTrail records all API calls and management events including root user sign-ins, and is the source of the sign-in event data, but does not itself send alerts or notifications when specific events occur without integration with CloudWatch Events or EventBridge. AWS Config continuously monitors resource configurations and evaluates compliance, and while it tracks resource state changes, it is not used to send real-time alerts for specific account login events such as root user console sign-ins. AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS compliance reports and certifications, and is a documentation portal with no capability to monitor or alert on AWS account activity or login events.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

### Question 380 (`CLF-U0350`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

How can a company separate costs for network traffic, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and other AWS services by department?

- **A)** Add department-specific tags to each resource
- **B)** Create a separate VPC for each department
- **C)** Create a separate AWS account for each department
- **D)** Use AWS Organizations

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

Creating a separate AWS account for each department provides the cleanest cost separation, as all charges within each account belong exclusively to that department and appear as a distinct line item on a consolidated bill.
Adding department-specific tags to each resource enables cost attribution within shared accounts through Cost Explorer, but tagging relies on consistent human application and does not provide the hard billing boundaries that separate accounts create. Creating a separate VPC for each department isolates network resources and can improve security, but VPCs do not create separate invoices or cost boundaries as all VPC resources still appear on the same AWS account bill. Using AWS Organizations provides account governance and consolidated billing but does not itself separate costs by department. It enables visibility across accounts but the cost separation comes from having distinct accounts rather than from Organizations itself.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>

### Question 382 (`CLF-U0569`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

A global company with a large number of AWS accounts is seeking a way in which they can centrally manage billing and security policies across all accounts. Which AWS Service will assist them in meeting these goals?

- **A)** AWS Organizations.
- **B)** AWS Trusted Advisor.
- **C)** IAM User Groups.
- **D)** AWS Config.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations provides centralized management of multiple AWS accounts, including consolidated billing and the ability to apply Service Control Policies as security guardrails across all accounts.
AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides recommendations across security, cost, performance, and fault tolerance, but operates at the individual account level and does not provide centralized management of billing or security policies across multiple accounts. IAM User Groups are a collection of IAM users that share the same attached policies within a single AWS account, and operate at the account level rather than providing cross-account billing or policy management. AWS Config continuously tracks and records the configuration of AWS resources to assess compliance and detect changes, but operates at the account level and does not provide cross-account billing management or security policy enforcement across an organization.

### Question 383 (`CLF-U0575`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

What is the AWS service that enables you to manage all of your AWS accounts from a single master account?

- **A)** AWS WAF.
- **B)** AWS Trusted Advisor.
- **C)** AWS Organizations.
- **D)** Amazon Config.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

**Correct answer: AWS Organizations**

AWS Organizations is an AWS service that allows you to centrally manage and govern multiple AWS accounts. It enables you to create organizational units (OUs), group accounts together, and apply policies across those accounts. This includes features like consolidated billing, which allows you to pay for all accounts in your organization from a single master account. You can also use service control policies (SCPs) to define guardrails and control which AWS services and actions are allowed in each account. This makes it easier to manage security, compliance, and resource allocation across your AWS environment.

**Incorrect:**

**A. Amazon Config** - Amazon Config is an AWS service that provides a detailed view of the configuration of AWS resources in your AWS accounts. It enables you to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your resources. While Config is useful for governance and compliance, it doesn't manage multiple accounts from a single master account in the way that AWS Organizations does.

**B. AWS Trusted Advisor** - AWS Trusted Advisor is an online tool that provides real-time guidance to help you provision your resources following AWS best practices. Trusted Advisor checks help optimize your AWS infrastructure, increase security and performance, reduce costs, and monitor service limits. It provides recommendations on individual accounts, but it doesn't manage multiple accounts from a single master account.

**C. AWS WAF** - AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) is a web application firewall that helps protect your web applications from common web exploits and bots. WAF can be deployed on Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, or Amazon API Gateway. While WAF is a crucial security service, it does not manage multiple AWS accounts from a single master account.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, ExamCert_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 384 (`CLF-U0591`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

AWS recommends some practices to help organizations avoid unexpected charges on their bill. Which of the following is NOT one of these practices?

- **A)** Deleting unused EBS volumes after terminating an EC2instance.
- **B)** Deleting unused AutoScaling launch configuration.
- **C)** Deleting unused Elastic Load Balancers.
- **D)** Releasing unused Elastic IPs after terminating an EC2instance.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

**Correct answer: Deleting unused AutoScaling launch configuration**

Deleting unused Auto Scaling launch configurations is a good practice for organization, but it does not directly impact AWS billing. Launch configurations are templates used to create EC2 instances within an Auto Scaling group. They don't consume resources or incur costs when they are not actively used by an Auto Scaling group. Therefore, keeping unused launch configurations around will not result in unexpected charges.

**Incorrect:**

**A. Deleting unused EBS volumes after terminating an EC2 instance** - EBS (Elastic Block Storage) volumes persist even after the EC2 instance they are attached to is terminated. If you don't delete these unused volumes, you will continue to be charged for the storage they consume. Deleting unused EBS volumes is a critical practice for cost optimization.

**B. Releasing unused Elastic IPs after terminating an EC2 instance** - Elastic IPs (EIPs) are static IPv4 addresses designed for dynamic cloud computing. While there's no charge for an Elastic IP when it's associated with a running EC2 instance, there is a small charge for Elastic IPs that are allocated but not associated with a running instance or are associated with a stopped instance. Releasing unused Elastic IPs is an important cost-saving measure.

**C. Deleting unused Elastic Load Balancers** - Elastic Load Balancers (ELBs) distribute incoming application traffic across multiple targets, such as EC2 instances. If you have an ELB that is no longer in use (i.e., no traffic is being routed through it), you will still be charged for it. Deleting unused ELBs is a key step in avoiding unnecessary costs.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, ExamCert_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 385 (`CLF-U0606`) [point:iam_role_temporary_credentials]

Which of the following has the greatest impact on cost? (Choose TWO)

- **A)** Compute charges.
- **B)** The number of services used.
- **C)** Data Transfer In charges.
- **D)** Data Transfer Out charges.
- **E)** The number of IAM roles provisioned.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A, D)</b></summary>

Compute charges and Data Transfer Out charges are typically the two largest cost drivers in AWS. Data Transfer In is free, and IAM roles have no associated cost.
The number of AWS services used does not directly determine cost impact. A single heavily used service can cost far more than dozens of lightly used services, so cost impact is driven by usage and pricing rates rather than the count of services consumed. Data Transfer In charges to AWS are free for all data ingested into the AWS network from the internet or from on-premises environments, making inbound data transfer one of the few cost components that does not contribute to the bill. The number of IAM roles provisioned incurs no charges. IAM roles are free to create and there is no per-role cost, so provisioning additional roles has no impact on your AWS bill.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 386 (`CLF-U0617`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

What are the benefits of the AWS Organizations service? (Choose TWO)

- **A)** Control access to AWS services.

<details>

AWS Organizations enables centralized control over AWS service access using Service Control Policies, and consolidates billing from multiple accounts into a single payment.
Helping organizations design and maintain an accelerated path to successful cloud adoption describes the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework, which is a guidance framework created by AWS Professional Services rather than a capability of AWS Organizations. Managing your organization's payment methods is handled through the AWS Billing and Cost Management console at the individual account level, and is not a specific feature provided by AWS Organizations. Helping organizations achieve their desired business outcomes with AWS describes AWS Professional Services, which works directly with customers on cloud strategy and implementation rather than being a function of AWS Organizations.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

### Question 387 (`CLF-U0632`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which AWS feature allows a company to take advantage of usage tiers for services across multiple member accounts?

- **A)** Service control policies (SCPs).
- **B)** Consolidated billing.
- **C)** All Upfront Reserved Instances.
- **D)** AWS Cost Explorer.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

Consolidated billing through AWS Organizations combines usage across all member accounts, allowing the organization to reach higher volume tiers and qualify for usage-based discounts that individual accounts would not achieve independently.
Service Control Policies are permission guardrails applied through AWS Organizations that restrict which AWS services and actions are available within member accounts, and are a governance mechanism rather than a feature that enables usage tier benefits. All Upfront Reserved Instances are a purchasing commitment where you pay the full cost of the reservation at the start of the term in exchange for the maximum discount, and apply to a single account rather than aggregating usage across multiple accounts. AWS Cost Explorer provides interactive visualisations and analysis of AWS spending patterns over time, and is a cost analysis tool rather than a feature that aggregates usage across accounts to qualify for volume pricing tiers.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 388 (`CLF-U0636`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which service allows a company with multiple AWS accounts to combine its usage to obtain volume discounts?

- **A)** AWS Server Migration Service.

- **D)** AWS Trusted Advisor.

AWS Organizations with consolidated billing combines usage across all member accounts, allowing the organization to qualify for volume pricing tiers and Reserved Instance sharing that individual accounts cannot achieve alone.
AWS Server Migration Service is a tool for migrating on-premises servers to AWS, and has no connection to combining usage across accounts or obtaining volume discounts. AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage thresholds and receive alerts when those thresholds are exceeded, and is a cost governance and alerting tool rather than a service that aggregates usage across accounts for volume discounts. AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides recommendations across security, cost, performance, and fault tolerance, and is an advisory tool rather than a service that combines usage across multiple accounts.

### Question 389 (`CLF-U0639`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

A customer is using multiple AWS accounts with separate billing. How can the customer take advantage of volume discounts with minimal impact to the AWS resources?

- **A)** Create one global AWS account and move all AWS resources to that account.
- **B)** Sign up for three years of Reserved Instance pricing up front.
- **C)** Use the consolidated billing feature from AWS Organizations.
- **D)** Sign up for the AWS Enterprise support plan to get volume discounts.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations consolidated billing aggregates usage across all member accounts, qualifying the organization for volume pricing tiers without requiring resource consolidation or upfront RI commitments.
Creating one global account and moving all resources is a high-impact change that would eliminate account-level isolation, security boundaries, and governance, and it is unnecessary because consolidated billing earns the same volume discounts without migration. Reserved Instance pricing locks compute into a specific instance type and term, which lowers cost for predictable workloads but does not provide cross-account volume discounts. The Enterprise Support plan adds Technical Account Managers and premium support, but support tiers do not grant volume discounts on service usage.

AWS Schema Conversion Tool is a database migration tool for converting database schemas between different engines, unrelated to account management. ### Question 391 (`CLF-U0669`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

How can one AWS account use Reserved Instances from another AWS account?

- **A)** By using Amazon EC2 Dedicated Instances.
- **B)** By using AWS Organizations consolidated billing.
- **C)** By using the AWS Cost Explorer tool.
- **D)** By using AWS Budgets.

<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations consolidated billing pools Reserved Instance usage across all member accounts, so unused RIs in one account can automatically apply to matching usage in another, reducing costs across the organization.
Amazon EC2 Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to a single customer for isolation and licensing purposes, and have no mechanism for sharing Reserved Instance discounts between accounts. The AWS Cost Explorer tool provides visualisation and analysis of AWS spending and usage patterns, and while it can show RI utilization data it cannot itself enable or facilitate RI sharing between accounts. AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage thresholds and receive alerts, and is a monitoring and governance tool with no capability to share Reserved Instance benefits across accounts.

</details>

### Question 392 (`CLF-U0672`) [point:comp_config_resource_rules]

A Cloud Practitioner must determine if any security groups in an AWS account have been provisioned to allow unrestricted access for specific ports. What is the SIMPLEST way to do this?

- **A)** Review the inbound rules for each security group in the Amazon EC2 management console to check for port 0.0.0.0/0.
- **B)** Run AWS Trusted Advisor and review the findings.
- **C)** Open the AWS IAM console and check the inbound rule filters for open access.
- **D)** In AWS Config, create a custom rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function to review firewall rules for inbound access.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

AWS Trusted Advisor automatically scans your account and flags security groups with unrestricted access (0.0.0.0/0) to specific ports as part of its Security category checks, making it the simplest and most direct approach without manual investigation.
Manually reviewing inbound rules for each security group in the EC2 console to look for 0.0.0.0/0 entries would work but is time-consuming and error-prone at scale, making it far less simple than using Trusted Advisor's automated check. The AWS IAM console manages identities, users, roles, and permissions, and does not contain security group configurations or inbound traffic rules, making it the wrong place to check for unrestricted port access. Creating a custom AWS Config rule that invokes a Lambda function to review firewall rules would provide automated ongoing compliance checks but requires significant setup effort, making it far more complex than running the existing Trusted Advisor check.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, DevOpsKing_Questions*

</details>

### Question 397 (`CLF-U0709`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which AWS service or feature allows a company to visualize, understand, and manage AWS costs and usage over time?

- **A)** AWS Budgets
- **B)** AWS Cost Explorer
- **C)** AWS Organizations
- **D)** Consolidated billing

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

AWS Cost Explorer provides interactive visualisations that let you understand, analyze, and manage your AWS costs and usage over time, with filtering, grouping, and forecasting capabilities.
AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage thresholds and receive alerts when those thresholds are exceeded, and is a proactive cost governance and alerting tool rather than a service for visualising and analyzing historical spending patterns. AWS Organizations provides centralized management of multiple AWS accounts including consolidated billing and Service Control Policies, and is an account governance service rather than a cost visualisation tool. Consolidated billing is a feature of AWS Organizations that combines usage and invoices from multiple accounts into a single bill, and is a billing aggregation feature rather than a tool for visualising and managing costs over time.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>

### Question 398 (`CLF-U0710`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which AWS service enables users to consolidate billing across multiple accounts?

- **A)** Amazon QuickSight
- **B)** AWS Organizations
- **C)** AWS Budgets
- **D)** Amazon Forecast

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations enables consolidated billing across multiple accounts, providing a single payment method and combined usage that can qualify for volume discounts.
Amazon QuickSight is a serverless business intelligence service for creating dashboards and visualisations from business data, and has no capability to consolidate billing across multiple AWS accounts. AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage thresholds and receive alerts when those thresholds are exceeded, and is a cost governance tool rather than a service that consolidates billing across accounts. Amazon Forecast is a machine learning service that generates time-series predictions such as demand or inventory forecasts, and is an AI analytics service with no connection to billing consolidation across AWS accounts.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

### Question 399 (`CLF-U0718`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which AWS service provides a quick and automated way to create and manage AWS accounts?

- **A)** AWS QuickSight
- **B)** Amazon Lightsail
- **C)** AWS Organizations
- **D)** Amazon Connect

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations provides automated account creation and centralized management of multiple AWS accounts, including consolidated billing, Service Control Policies, and organizational units.
AWS QuickSight is a serverless business intelligence service for creating dashboards and visualisations from business data, and has no capability to create or manage AWS accounts. Amazon Lightsail is a simplified compute service for deploying virtual servers and web applications with straightforward pricing, and is a compute service rather than an account management tool. Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service for managing customer communications via voice and chat, and is a customer engagement service with no connection to AWS account creation or management.

### Question 400 (`CLF-U0725`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

A company has multiple AWS accounts within AWS Organizations and wants to apply the Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances benefit to a single account only. Which action should be taken?

- **A)** Purchase the Reserved Instances from master payer account and turn off Reserved Instance sharing.
- **B)** Enable billing alerts in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.
- **C)** Purchase the Reserved Instances in individual linked accounts and turn off Reserved Instance sharing from the payer level.
- **D)** Enable Reserved Instance sharing in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: A)</b></summary>

To restrict Reserved Instance benefits to a single account, purchase the RIs from the master payer account and turn off Reserved Instance sharing in the billing settings, preventing the discounts from applying to other member accounts.
Enabling billing alerts in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console creates notifications when spending exceeds thresholds, and has no effect on how Reserved Instance benefits are shared or restricted across accounts in an organization. Purchasing the Reserved Instances in individual linked accounts and turning off RI sharing from the payer level would apply RI restrictions organization-wide rather than limiting benefits to a single specific account. Enabling Reserved Instance sharing in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console would expand RI benefit sharing across all member accounts, which is the opposite of restricting the benefit to a single account.

*Sources: AwsCcpTrainer_Questions, CloudCertPrep_Questions*

</details>

### Question 401 (`CLF-U0731`) [point:iam_role_temporary_credentials]

Each department within a company has its own independent AWS account and its own payment method. New company leadership wants to centralize departmental governance and consolidate payments. How can this be achieved using AWS services or features?

- **A)** Forward monthly invoices for each account. Then create IAM roles to allow cross-account access.
- **B)** Create a new AWS account. Then configure AWS Organizations and invite all existing accounts to join.
- **C)** Configure AWS Organizations in each of the existing accounts. Then link all accounts together.
- **D)** Use Cost Explorer to combine costs from all accounts. Then replicate IAM policies across accounts.

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: B)</b></summary>

Creating a new AWS account and configuring AWS Organizations allows you to invite existing accounts to join, enabling centralized governance through Service Control Policies and consolidated billing under a single payer account.
Forwarding monthly invoices and creating IAM roles for cross-account access addresses reporting and permissions separately, but does not centralize governance or consolidate payments into a single billing structure under a payer account. AWS Organizations can only have one management account within an organization, and configuring it in multiple existing accounts simultaneously is not possible. The correct approach is to configure it in a single management account and then invite others to join. Using Cost Explorer to combine cost views and replicating IAM policies across accounts provides some visibility and consistency, but does not centralize governance through SCPs or consolidate payments into a single invoice the way AWS Organizations does.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>

### Question 402 (`CLF-U0732`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which tool is used to forecast AWS spending?

- **A)** AWS Trusted Advisor
- **B)** AWS Organizations
- **C)** Cost Explorer
- **D)** Amazon Inspector

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

AWS Cost Explorer provides cost forecasting capabilities that use historical spending data to project future AWS expenses, helping organizations anticipate and plan for upcoming costs.
AWS Trusted Advisor analyzes your environment and provides recommendations across security, cost, performance, and fault tolerance, and is an advisory tool for optimizing existing deployments rather than a forecasting service for future spending. AWS Organizations provides centralized account management with consolidated billing and governance controls, and is an account structure and governance service rather than a tool for forecasting future AWS spending. Amazon Inspector is an automated security assessment service that scans EC2 instances and container images for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, and is a security tool with no cost forecasting capability.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

### Question 403 (`CLF-U0738`) [point:iam_mfa_root_account]

A user needs to generate a report that outlines the status of key security checks in an AWS account. The report must include: (The status of Amazon S3 bucket permissions, Whether multi-factor authentication is enabled for the AWS account root user, If any security groups are configured to allow unrestricted access.) Where can all this information be found in one location?

- **A)** Amazon QuickSight dashboard
- **B)** AWS CloudTrail trails
- **C)** AWS Trusted Advisor report
- **D)** IAM credential report

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: C)</b></summary>

AWS Trusted Advisor provides a report-style dashboard of check results across security, cost, performance, fault tolerance, and service limits, including key security checks such as MFA on root account, exposed access keys, and open security groups.
Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence and data visualisation service for creating dashboards and reports from data sources, and while it can display data, it does not provide automated AWS security check results or account-level security status summaries. AWS CloudTrail trails record API calls and account activity for auditing purposes, and while they capture security-relevant events, they produce raw logs rather than a summarized status report of key security check findings. The IAM credential report lists all IAM users and the status of their credentials including password age, access key status, and MFA enablement, and while it is a useful security tool, it covers only IAM credential status rather than the broader set of key security checks that Trusted Advisor evaluates.

### Question 404 (`CLF-U0740`) [point:orgs_service_control_policies]

Which features and benefits does the AWS Organizations service provide? (Choose two.)

- **A)** Establishing real-time communications between members of an internal team
- **B)** Facilitating the use of NoSQL databases
- **C)** Providing automated security checks
- **D)** Implementing consolidated billing
- **E)** Enforcing the governance of AWS accounts

<details>
<summary><b>View Answer & Rationale (Answer: D, E)</b></summary>

AWS Organizations implements consolidated billing to combine multiple accounts under one payment method, and enforces governance through Service Control Policies that restrict which services and actions are available within member accounts.
Establishing real-time communications between members of an internal team is the function of collaboration tools such as Amazon Chime or AWS Wickr, not AWS Organizations, which manages account structure and billing. Facilitating the use of NoSQL databases is the function of services such as Amazon DynamoDB, which provides managed NoSQL database capabilities, rather than AWS Organizations which is an account management service. Providing automated security checks is the function of services such as Amazon Inspector, AWS Security Hub, and Amazon GuardDuty, rather than AWS Organizations which focuses on account governance and billing consolidation.

*Sources: CloudCertPrep_Questions, AwsCcpTrainer_Questions*

</details>
